abstract.p: Manufacturing is resource- and emission-intensive, yet the sustainability returns to digitalisation are uneven and far from automatic. This study develops a framework explaining how, and under what conditions, digital twin capability (DTC) may contribute to sustainable business performance (SBP), with business competitiveness (BC) proposed as the mediating mechanism. Drawing on the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and digital transformation theory, DTC is conceptualised as a firm-level capability comprising real-time monitoring (RTM), predictive simulation (PSM), process synchronisation (PSY) and intelligent decision support (IDS). SBP is operationalised through environmental, social, and governance (ESG) pillars, kept conceptually separate from the economic content of competitiveness. The framework was demonstrated with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) on an illustrative dataset of 418 cases created for demonstration rather than collected from manufacturing firms. In the illustrative estimation, DTC was positively associated with BC (β = 0.54, p < 0.001), which was positively associated with SBP (β = 0.44, p < 0.001). The direct path from DTC to SBP was not significant (β = 0.06, p = 0.238), whereas the indirect path through competitiveness was significant (β = 0.24, p < 0.001; 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.19, 0.30]), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. At the pillar level, competitiveness was associated with environmental (β = 0.45, p < 0.001) and governance performance (β = 0.39, p < 0.001) but not with social performance (β = 0.02, p = 0.713). These estimates are illustrative only and are intended to demonstrate the potential for assessing these proposed relationships but do not confirm their existence or size and field validation is necessary, especially in Jordanian manufacturing. The study redefines the digital twin as an organizational capability, outlines what competitiveness is as a testable sustainability mechanism and provides a design at the pillar level that can reveal the disparities that lie behind composite measures.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Manufacturing lies at the centre of the sustainability challenge. Industrial production converts large volumes of energy and materials into products, emissions and waste. Manufacturers are increasingly expected to account not only for these environmental burdens but also for occupational safety, workforce development, community relations and the quality of their governance (Elkington, 1997; Gillan et al., 2021). Sustainability performance across manufacturing firms is, however, uneven. Improvements in one dimension do not necessarily carry over to others, and the sustainability consequences of new production technologies vary considerably across technologies and industries (Bai et al., 2020; Narkhede et al., 2024). Understanding what produces such uneven outcomes is therefore a central question for sustainable manufacturing.

Digital transformation is frequently presented as part of the answer. Industry 4.0 technologies, such as cyber-physical systems, the industrial Internet of Things, artificial intelligence and advanced analytics, promise production that is more efficient, more transparent and easier to control (Dalenogare et al., 2018; Frank et al., 2019). Ghobakhloo (2020) identifies a range of sustainability functions that Industry 4.0 may perform, from production efficiency to energy sustainability, emission reduction and social welfare. Digitalisation, however, is not inherently sustainable. Digital infrastructure consumes energy and materials, and efficiency gains can be offset by growth and rebound effects (Lange et al., 2020). Automation and work intensification can also generate social tensions, such as job displacement and widening skill gaps (Kovacs, 2018; Narkhede et al., 2024). Whether digital investment advances sustainable manufacturing therefore depends on how it is embedded in organisational activity rather than on adoption as such (Vial, 2019).

Digital twins are a particularly relevant case. A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical asset, process or system that is continuously updated through bidirectional data exchange with its physical counterpart (Grieves & Vickers, 2017; Kritzinger et al., 2018; Tao et al., 2019). Because it links sensing to simulation and decision-making, a digital twin offers mechanisms with direct sustainability relevance. These mechanisms include real-time monitoring (RTM) of energy and material flows and predictive maintenance that extends asset life and reduces scrap. They also include the simulation of scenarios whose resource and emission consequences can be evaluated before physical changes are made, and data-driven control that supports traceability and accountability (He & Bai, 2021; Kamble et al., 2022). Case-based research reports reductions in unit energy consumption and environmental protection costs from digital-twin-enabled production management (Ma et al., 2022). Design studies further document digital twin applications in energy-efficiency monitoring, carbon-footprint analysis and circular production (He et al., 2023; Preut et al., 2021; Zeynivand et al., 2025).

These mechanisms are, however, technical potentials rather than realised outcomes. Firms that possess similar digital twin technologies may achieve very different sustainability results. Before the technology can shape environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, it must first be converted into organisational routines, competitive outcomes and resource commitments.

Firm-level research has begun to examine this conversion. Digital twin adoption has been associated with supply-chain sustainability through supply-chain resilience and performance (Singh et al., 2023), and digital twin innovation has been associated with higher operational performance (Li et al., 2026). Nevertheless, two questions remain insufficiently theorised and tested: the organisational mechanism through which digital twin capability (DTC) may translate into sustainable business performance (SBP), and whether that mechanism operates equally across ESG outcomes.

This study proposes business competitiveness (BC) as that mechanism. Competitiveness is understood here as cost efficiency, service quality and reliability, market and customer relationships, and innovation and technological adaptation. It is the proximate outcome that a digital twin is designed to improve. It is also a potential source of the financial slack, legitimacy and operational discipline that firms need to sustain environmental and governance commitments (Hart, 1995; Porter, 1985).

A competitiveness-based pathway is, however, unlikely to benefit all sustainability dimensions equally. Efficiency-oriented competitiveness may align closely with resource efficiency and governance. Social outcomes, by contrast, depend heavily on labour practices, workforce development and institutional conditions that competitiveness does not necessarily change (Narkhede et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2021). The study therefore investigates both the pathway through which DTC may contribute to SBP and the conditions under which this pathway does or does not reach each sustainability dimension.

Jordan provides the intended application context for the framework. Jordanian manufacturing is an emerging-economy setting in which digital transformation is advancing unevenly. Survey evidence indicates that organisational culture, information technology (IT) readiness and customer demands shape the adoption of digital transformation among Jordanian manufacturers, and that adoption is associated with improved operational performance (Almajali et al., 2025). Evidence from other Jordanian sectors points in the same direction. Business intelligence adoption in e-banking depends on identifiable organisational and technological drivers and faces distinct implementation challenges (Alzubi, 2025), and the professional use of digital social platforms has been linked to talent-acquisition effectiveness in tourism firms (Momani et al., 2026). Comparable evidence from manufacturing sectors in other developing countries shows that technological, organisational and environmental conditions shape Industry 4.0 adoption and its performance consequences (Al-Amin et al., 2024). Such variation in readiness makes the conversion of digital capability into sustainability outcomes an important question for this context. The present study does not, however, analyse data from Jordanian firms. Instead, the framework is demonstrated with an illustrative dataset of 418 cases, created to show how the measurement and structural models can be estimated and evaluated. Jordan is therefore treated as the setting for subsequent field validation, not as the source of the reported estimates.

The study has four aims: (i) to conceptualise DTC as a multidimensional, firm-level capability relevant to sustainable manufacturing; (ii) to theorise the pathway from DTC to SBP through BC; (iii) to specify a pillar-level design that can detect differences in how ESG performance respond to competitiveness; and (iv) to demonstrate the operationalisation and evaluation of the framework with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) using illustrative data. Throughout, the paper distinguishes between what is theoretically proposed, what is illustrated with the 418-case dataset and what can be established only through future field research.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews research on digital twins and sustainable manufacturing, develops the DTC construct and clarifies the relationship between SBP, ESG criteria and the triple bottom line. Section 3 sets out the theoretical foundation, and Section 4 develops the hypotheses. Section 5 describes the methodology and the status of the illustrative dataset, and Section 6 reports the illustrative estimation. Section 7 discusses the results, Section 8 presents the implications, Section 9 addresses the limitations and directions for future research, and Section 10 concludes.

sec.title: 2.1. Digital twins and sustainable manufacturing
sec.p: The research landscape regarding digital twins for manufacturing has grown primarily in the field of engineering and operations management, and an increasing fraction of this research tackled sustainability outcomes directly. This study is related to four streams.

The first stream is related to resource and energy efficiency. Digital Twins, which provide RTM and failure prediction for manufacturing equipment, systems and services, are regarded as pillars of sustainable intelligent manufacturing by He & Bai (2021). Ma et al. (2022) offer a digital twin and “big data” approach for energy intensive industries. In two of the firm’s cases, they cite decreases in unit energy usage and energy cost in one company and significant decreases in environmental protection cost in the other. Zeynivand et al. (2025) design a real-time digital twin of a machine tool to track energy consumption of the machine with respect to machining parameters and estimate energy consequences of bearing faults at the machine level. Their model thus connects the predictive maintenance with energy-saving operation.

The second stream is related to environmental performance and emissions. He et al. (2023) apply carbon-footprint analysis to a closed-loop digital twin in the context of making low-carbon products. Hafeez et al. (2024) conclude that digital twins can help electrification and the utilization of zero carbon fuels, but that the low reliability of models and the high initial investment in IT today restricts adoption, especially for hard-to-abate industries. The finding is of particular relevance for the present study as it highlights the dependency of the potential of the digital twins on the organisational and financial situation.

The third stream has to do with circular production. Preut et al. (2021) state that product and process information which can be provided by digital twins is required to implement circular supply chains, but product- and use-case-specific implementations still need to be developed. Kristoffersen et al. (2020) associate circular-economy strategies with the analytics needed for their delivery. According to views among industry experts, the industry moves towards circularity because of the confluence of industry stakeholders, regulatory and competitive pressures, with digital twin opportunities in product design, use, decommissioning and renewal (Timperi et al., 2024).

The fourth stream examines sustainable operations and firm-level outcomes. Kamble et al. (2022) synthesise research on digital twins for sustainable manufacturing supply chains and propose an implementation framework that extends the digital twin beyond single plants to the wider supply chain. Survey-based research remains limited but is growing. In a PLS-SEM study of manufacturing supply-chain professionals, Singh et al. (2023) find that digital twin adoption is associated with supply-chain sustainability through supply-chain resilience and performance. Li et al. (2026) report large-sample evidence that digital twin innovation is associated with higher operational performance, with stronger effects in firms with greater financial slack and in more dynamic industries. At the broader level of digital transformation, Jin & Wu (2024) find that digital transformation improves the ESG performance of Chinese state-owned manufacturers through dynamic-capability mechanisms. Fan et al. (2025) report that digital technology application raises enterprise competitiveness, with ESG performance and green technology innovation exerting suppressing effects on that relationship. Lan & Zhou (2024) show that digitalisation and ESG strategies jointly support firm innovation, but that this joint effect becomes substitutive in resource-constrained firms such as small and medium-sized enterprises and firms facing high financing constraints. Digitalisation can also carry risks across the supply chain: Chen et al. (2025) find that misalignment in digital transformation levels between suppliers and buyers increases supplier financial risk.

Three features of this literature shape the present study. First, most evidence connecting digital twins with sustainability derives from engineering designs, case studies and reviews, and it concerns asset- or process-level functions rather than firm-level capability. Second, firm-level survey studies are few, and many examine Industry 4.0 or digital transformation in general rather than digital twins specifically (e.g., Bag et al., 2021; Jin & Wu, 2024). Third, sustainability outcomes are usually either limited to the environmental dimension or aggregated into a single index; social and governance outcomes are rarely separated. At the same time, research on the rebound effects of digitalisation (Lange et al., 2020) and on the negative side of Industry 4.0 (Kovacs, 2018; Narkhede et al., 2024) cautions against assuming that the technical sustainability potential of digital twins is realised automatically.

sec.title: 2.2. From digital twin technology to digital twin capability
sec.p: A lot of the literature refers to the digital twin as a technological artefact made up of sensors, connectivity, modelling platforms and analytics. Kritzinger et al. (2018) differentiate between the digital model, the digital shadow and the digital twin based on the levels of automatic data integration between the physical and virtual objects. A digital twin is only a digital twin when data flows back and forth between the two. This separation brings clarity on what a digital twin is, but not to the question of which companies can do it better than others. This study follows the capacity approach to digital transformation (Warner & Wäger, 2019) to identify DTC, which is the capacity of a firm to deploy digital twins to represent, anticipate, coordinate and improve its physical operations. DTC is viewed on four dimensions which collectively cover the lifecycle of a digital twin.

RTM records the state of physical operations at the time. Deviations can be seen without manual inspection as sensor-enabled data on machine status, energy use, and throughput are continually transferred into a virtual representation (Tao et al., 2019). The informational dimension upon which the other functions rely.

Predictive simulation (PSM) enables companies to forecast results and test situations. Model-based forecasting and “what if” analysis help companies simulate equipment failure, understand how changes in demand or production processes affect production and resource consumption without physically testing the setup, or try out setups virtually before making the real investment (Lu et al., 2020; Qi & Tao, 2018).

Process synchronisation (PSY) links physical and digital states between operational systems. It ensures that data are consistent across machines, lines and plants, integrated with planning and execution systems like enterprise resource planning (ERP) and manufacturing execution systems (MES) and remains consistent as conditions change (Kritzinger et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2020). This dimension refers to the bi-directional coupling and differentiates a digital twin from a digital shadow.

Intelligent decision support (IDS) translates the digital twin data into managerial and operational decisions. The recommendations derived from analytics are used to inform scheduling, resource allocation and assessing trade-offs, making the loop from representation to action (Kamble et al., 2022; Tao et al., 2019).

The four dimensions are sequential, functioning as a sort of process: sensing the present, anticipating the future, coordinating physical and digital states, and acting on the resulting information. For two reasons they are considered as a part of a capability rather than two separate technologies. They are interdependent with the same data infrastructure, competence in modelling and integration, and value pertaining to sustainability emerges from their combination. Monitoring without simulation gives visibility but no foresight and simulation without decision support gives foresight but no action. Concurrently, the dimensions are conceptually complementary, and so a reflective–formative specification might also be justified; the implications of this choice for measurement are considered in Section 5.5.

Some related concepts are intentionally not modeled as dimensions of DTC. Technical pre-conditions for RTM and PSY are interoperability and data integration quality, which determine the possibility of implementing these functions but are not part of the digital twin’s purpose. Organisational antecedents are factors that must be prepared in an organisation before the process of digital transformation can take place, and digital skills are factors that can enhance the process of digital transformation. In Jordanian manufacturing, for instance, digital skills along with organisational culture and IT readiness are considered to be organisational antecedents for digital transformation (Almajali et al., 2025). Information technology infrastructure is a common enabling resource that is shared by various Industry 4.0 applications. These as dimensions would merge the capability with its enabling conditions and lead to confusion around DTC and general Industry 4.0 capability. They should thus be reserved for future extensions of the framework under the sections of antecedents, moderators or contextual factors.

sec.title: 2.3. Sustainable business performance, the triple bottom line and environment, social, and governance
sec.p: In the literature on corporate sustainability, three different but related frameworks are found. The triple bottom line (Elkington, 1997) measures a business’ performance on economic, environmental and social metrics, and it suggests that the purpose of a business is not just to make money, but to create value in other ways as well. ESG is a term that is used to describe the environmental, social, and governance criteria used for evaluating the sustainability-related performance and risks of companies, including investors and other stakeholders (Gillan et al., 2021). While they share environmental and social features, the two frameworks have two key distinctions. First, the triple bottom line has a component of economic performance, which is not present in the ESG. Secondly, ESG considers governance (transparency, accountability, ethics and risk management) as a separate leg, while the triple bottom line does not. The two frameworks are thus not synonymous but related.

SBP in this study is defined as a company’s performance on sustainability-related outcomes that go beyond its financial and market performance. It is worth to note that SBP is not implemented in the economic–environmental–social framework of the triple bottom line, but through the pillars of environment, social, and governance (ESG) for two reasons. The construct of BC already includes the economic and competitive performance as cost efficiency, market share, customer relationships and innovation.

The addition of an economic pillar to SBP will create conceptual overlap and unrealistically boost the competitiveness–sustainability path, since the outcome will contain the same content as in the mediator. Second, governance is also relevant to DTC as it is possible to use data-driven monitoring and risk management to improve traceability and accountability. This operationalisation, however, is in an ESG direction, which enables the examination of ESG outcomes separately from the economic performance, which stays within the mediator side of the model.

“SBP” is therefore an indicator of sustainable business performance that can be translated into an operationalisation of ESG. Does not constitute an external ESG rating and is not a restatement of the triple bottom line. Due to the fact that the three pillars reflect other areas, they do not need to go together and a composite measure may mask pillar-level results that are divergent (Narkhede et al., 2024). Hence, the framework examines the overall SBP result as well as each pillar independently.

sec.title: 2.4. The mechanism of business competitiveness as a sustainability-relevant mechanism
sec.p: BC is the performance of a business to generate more value for customers and stakeholders than its competitors (Porter, 1985). This study follows the same approach as the previous study to define the concept of BC within the manufacturing sector in four dimensions: cost efficiency, service quality and reliability, market and customer relationships, and innovation and technological adaptation, in line with the expectations for the contribution of Industry 4.0 (Dalenogare et al., 2018). A digital twin is most directly being designed to achieve these outcomes, making BC a likely intervening mechanism between DTC and sustainability outcomes.

For three reasons, BC is relevant to sustainable transition and not just to firm performance. First, competitive firms have the financial resources to invest in environmental and social projects whose benefits are uncertain or delayed (Hart, 1995). Second, quality and reliable suppliers better position themselves to meet environmental and governance requirements which the customer is increasingly demanding, innovations and technological adaptation offer the ability to adopt cleaner processes. Thirdly, Ghobakhloo (2020) reveals that the economic sustainability role of Industry 4.0 (production efficiency, business-model innovation, etc.) comes before and underpins its environmental and social sustainability role.

There is, however, an uncertainty about the competitiveness–sustainability relationship. The ESG performance will be modeled by Fan et al. (2025) as an intermediate link between digital technology application and competitiveness, while the natural-resource-based view proposes that competitive resources will support sustainability commitments (Hart, 1995). Theoretically, either of the two orderings or both can be in effect. This study proposes BC as a mediator between DTC and SBP, which is a theoretically driven statement. It is not saying this ordering is realised and cross-sectional data cannot determine between the two orderings.

sec.title: 2.5. State of the evidence and research gap
sec.p: Table 1 summarises which relationships in the proposed framework are supported by prior research, which are theoretically proposed but insufficiently tested, and which are specifically integrated by this study.

The review identifies a substantive theory gap. Previous studies describe the technical capabilities of digital twins in the area of sustainability and demonstrate the potential for digitalisation to affect ESG results. It does not include, however, an account of the organizational mechanism that connects the DTC of a firm to its sustainability outcomes, or of why this mechanism may connect to some aspects of sustainability and not to others. If it weren’t for such an account, it would be hard to explain why the outcomes of sustainability investments with similar digital twins are so different, or where sustainability returns are likely not to show up. This needs to be addressed with (i) a capability-based conceptualisation of digital twins, (ii) a theorised conversion mechanism and (iii) a pillar-level view of sustainability outcomes.
The study addresses three research questions (RQs):
RQ1: Through what pathway may DTC contribute to SBP: directly, indirectly through BC, or both?
RQ2: Does the competitiveness pathway extend equally to ESG performance?
RQ3: How can the proposed framework be operationalised and evaluated with PLS-SEM before field validation?

sec.title: 3. Theoretical foundation
sec.p: The framework draws on three theoretical lenses, each of which addresses a different question. The resource-based view explains why DTC can be strategically valuable. Dynamic capabilities theory explains how DTC is converted into competitive outcomes. Digital transformation theory explains how digital capabilities become broader organisational and performance outcomes, including sustainability outcomes.

sec.title: 3.1. Resource-based view: why digital twin capability can be strategically valuable
sec.p: According to resource-based view, a sustainable competitive advantage is based on valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable resources (Barney, 1991). The technology itself (a digital twin platform) does not satisfy these requirements, as the software can be bought. DTC, however, is integrating the tech with its data assets, process models, integration expertise and decision routines. They are built over time, particular to the firm’s operations and hard for competitors to be able to observe or replicate. The natural-resource-based view further takes this argument: the more a firm is capable of pollution prevention and resource stewardship, the more it will be able to gain advantage (Hart, 1995); and empirical studies in this field showed that the critical resources of Industry 4.0 are associated with sustainable production (Bag et al., 2021). The resource-based view thus sets the foundations for considering DTC as a strategic and sustainability-related resource with the potential to enhance competitive position. It does not however, account for how this potential is realized.

sec.title: 3.2. Dynamic capabilities theory: how digital twin capability is converted into competitiveness
sec.p: Dynamic capabilities theory describes how the firm detects opportunities and threats and adapts by adjusting its resources commitments and restructuring its resource portfolio in response to changing conditions (Teece et al., 1997; Teece, 2007). These microfoundations are connected to the four DTC dimensions. Sensing is supported by both RTM and PSM, as both show deviations, predict failures and predict the implications of changes in demand or process conditions. IDS helps the managers identify options and resource allocations for seizing. Because PSY allows for coordinated adjustments across interdependent production stages, it makes it possible to reconfigure. Digital Sensing, Seizing and Transforming capabilities are crucial to digital transformation as demonstrated in Warner & Wäger (2019). The first step of the proposed pathway is the transformation of DTC into lower costs, higher reliability, higher responsiveness and faster adaptation, which can be explained by the dynamic capabilities theory.

sec.title: 3.3. Digital transformation theory: how digital capability becomes organisational and sustainability outcomes
sec.p: Digital transformation theory conceptualises digital technologies as triggers for strategic responses that alter a firm’s value-creation paths. It emphasises that performance outcomes depend on structural and organisational change rather than on the technology itself (Verhoef et al., 2021; Vial, 2019). Two implications follow for this study. First, sustainability returns from DTC are expected to arise mainly as the capability reshapes operational and competitive routines, rather than directly from the technology; the direct DTC–SBP path is therefore expected to be weak relative to the indirect path. Second, outcomes depend on which routines are reorganised. Digital twins reorganise efficiency, quality and control routines, which are closely linked to environmental and governance outcomes. Social outcomes, by contrast, depend on human-resource, participation and safety routines that DTC-driven competitiveness does not necessarily change.

sec.title: 3.4. Integrated causal logic
sec.p: Together, the three lenses form a single causal chain rather than three parallel explanations. DTC is a strategically valuable resource (resource-based view). It is converted into BC through sensing, seizing and reconfiguring (dynamic capabilities theory). BC is, in turn, translated into sustainability outcomes through reorganised routines and resource commitments whose reach differs across the ESG domains (digital transformation theory, supported by the natural-resource-based view). sec.title: 4. Hypotheses development
sec.p: Building on this logic, the framework proposes that DTC contributes to SBP mainly through BC, and that the competitiveness pathway may differ across the ESG pillars.

sec.title: 4.1. Digital twin capability and business competitiveness
sec.p: In terms of dynamic capabilities, DTC enhances the sources of competitive advantage in the immediate vicinity. RTM and predictive maintenance minimize downtime, scrap and rework, which decreases operating costs. Synchronised control enhances the quality and reliability of delivery, scenario simulation boosts responsiveness to changes in customer demand, and decision support speeds technological adaptation (Lu et al., 2020; Teece, 2007). At least one DTC dimension caters to one dimension of BC, and so on. Firm-level evidence also supports this argument: Digital twin innovation has been found to be related to higher operational performance (Li et al., 2026), while digital twin adoption with supply-chain performance (Singh et al., 2023). The impact of digital capability on operational and manufacturing performance is also found in the literature on the broader digital transformation of Jordanian manufacturing (Almajali et al., 2025) as well as in the adoption of Industry 4.0 in other developing-country contexts (Al-Amin et al., 2024). Likewise, Industry 4.0 technologies and information integration have been linked to better logistics performance, and the digital transformation has conditioned this link (Banihani et al., 2026).
H1: Digital twin capability has a positive effect on BC.

sec.title: 4.2. Business competitiveness and sustainable business performance
sec.p: Competitive firms possess resources that enable sustainability investment. Financial slack allows them to fund environmental and social initiatives with uncertain or delayed returns. Market legitimacy and stable customer relationships create incentives to meet the sustainability expectations of stakeholders. In addition, the operational discipline associated with cost efficiency and quality management supports the institutionalisation of environmental and governance practices (Hart, 1995; Porter, 1985). The finding by Ghobakhloo (2020) that economic sustainability functions precede and enable environmental and social functions supports this ordering. BC is therefore expected to act as a proximal enabler of SBP rather than merely as its correlate.
H2: BC has a positive effect on SBP.

sec.title: 4.3. Direct effect of digital twin capability on sustainable business performance
sec.p: DTC may also affect sustainability outcomes directly, independently of any change in competitive position. Energy monitoring, predictive maintenance and process optimisation can reduce resource consumption and emissions even when these gains are not yet reflected in costs or market position (He & Bai, 2021; Ma et al., 2022). Comparable evidence from logistics shows that smart technologies and cognitive computing are associated with better environmental performance, with predictive and forecasting analytics acting as mediating mechanisms (Alqudah et al., 2025a; Alqudah et al., 2025b). Digital transformation theory, however, implies that most sustainability returns arise through organisational change rather than through technology alone (Vial, 2019), and rebound effects may offset direct efficiency gains (Lange et al., 2020). The direct path is therefore specified to test whether any sustainability effect of DTC remains once the competitiveness pathway is taken into account.
H3: Digital twin capability has a positive direct effect on SBP.

sec.title: 4.4. Mediating role of business competitiveness
sec.p: H1 and H2 together suggest an indirect pathway whereby the strength of BC is reinforced by DTC and the strength of SBP is reinforced by BC. The first step in this pathway could be explained by dynamic capabilities theory, and the second step by digital transformation theory (Teece, 2007; Verhoef et al., 2021). Mediation is determined by the significance of the indirect effect, as recommended in the present mediation analysis literature (Nitzl et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2010). If the direct effect is significant then its significance dictates whether the pattern is complementary (both are significant and of the same sign) or indirect – only (direct not significant, but indirect is significant).
H4: BC mediates the relationship between DTC and SBP.

sec.title: 4.5. Pillar-specific effects of business competitiveness
sec.p: The impact of BC is explored on each of the ESG pillars as they represent different areas. The improved competitiveness due to efficiency has a huge overlap with environmental performance, in that greater resource productivity (less energy and material consumption per unit of product) yields lower costs and environmental impacts. Competitive firms with demanding customers are likely to institutionalize control, traceability and disclosure mechanisms, which will ultimately improve governance performance, and where firms are data-driven, this is likely to be reinforced (Jin & Wu, 2024). The link with social performance is theoretically less certain. Human-resource practices, employee participation, labour regulation, and institutional conditions are among the critical factors that influence social outcomes like occupational safety, employee development, fair labour practices, and community contribution (Xu et al., 2021). Efficiency and cost reduction based competitiveness can be combined with work intensification or limited social investment (Kovacs, 2018; Narkhede et al., 2024). However, the three hypotheses are written in a positive way, testing the pillars in a symmetrical fashion, not on a “prejudged expectation”.
H5: BC has a positive effect on environmental performance.
H6: BC has a positive effect on social performance.
H7: BC has a positive effect on governance performance.

sec.title: 4.6. Conceptual framework
sec.p: Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework. DTC is linked to BC (H1), which is linked to SBP (H2). A direct path from DTC to SBP is also specified (H3), and BC is proposed to mediate the relationship between DTC and SBP (H4). In a disaggregated specification, SBP is replaced by its three pillars so that the effect of BC on ESG performance can be tested separately (H5–H7).

sec.title: 5.1. Research design and status of the illustrative dataset
sec.p: This study is deductive in nature, employs a quantitative research method, and has a cross sectional design for the evaluation of relationships between latent constructs. The analytical nature of each part of the study is explicitly indicated as the Empirical component is not based on field observations but rather on an illustrative dataset.
Theoretically proposed. The constructs, their sizes, the causal logic and hypotheses H1–H7 (Sections 2–4).

With the 418 case data set illustrated. The operationalisation of the constructs, the evaluation of the measurement model, the estimation of the structural model and the testing of mediation (Section 6). How the framework can be estimated, how its diagnostics are assessed, and how decisions on hypotheses are made, is illustrated.

Established with future field research. The proposed relationships are examined in terms of whether they are actually present, and if so how strong, among manufacturing firms (including Jordanian manufacturing firms); whether the instrument includes content and construct validity; and whether the pattern observed is generalisable.

The 418 cases are an illustrative sample used to illustrate the proposed model. They were not gathered from manufacturing companies, managers or any other respondents and fieldwork was not done. The cases are not a representative sample of Jordanian manufacturers or any other sub-population. No firm characteristics, respondent demographics or response rates are reported since no firm or respondent characteristics or response rates exist. The coefficients reported in Section 6 are thus only illustrative and refer to the illustrative data set. The resulting patterns (including the non-significant patterns) were not intended to be used as discoveries about the behavior of the firms, as the data was created for demonstration purposes. Instead, they demonstrate that the model described can be estimated and its hypotheses could be judged as would be done in a field application.

sec.title: 5.2. Intended empirical context and target population
sec.p: The framework is applicable for use in the future in the manufacturing sector in Jordan. The target companies include companies in the following main industrial sectors: chemicals &amp; pharmaceuticals, food &amp; beverages, plastics &amp; packaging, engineering &amp; electrical industries, construction materials. Theoretically, Jordan is relevant to the study of digital transformation among its manufacturers as a result of different organisational culture, IT readiness and customer demands (Almajali et al., 2025). The framework is likely to generate the variation in DTC that these conditions will generate.

The unit of analysis is the firm in the planned field study. Key informants are senior managers who have hands-on experience with operations and digital initiatives and include operations managers, production managers, supply chain managers, plant managers and digital-transformation managers. To gain greater coverage of the population, a purposive sampling procedure is planned, with stratification by sub-sector and firm size. An a priori power analysis was conducted in G*Power with f² = 0.15, α = 0.05 and power = 0.95. This analysis used a conservative number of predictors (three), but the maximum number of any endogenous construct in the model was two, and the minimum number required was 119 firms. This field protocol has not been instituted yet.

sec.title: 5.3. Illustrative dataset
sec.p: The illustrative dataset contains 418 cases measured on the 44 indicators described in Section 5.4. Its size exceeds the minimum sample indicated by the power analysis and supports stable bootstrap estimation. Because the cases do not correspond to actual firms, the dataset carries no information on sub-sector, firm size or respondent characteristics. The sole purpose of the dataset is to demonstrate the estimation and evaluation procedure. Field estimation using the protocol in Section 5.2 is required before any coefficient can be interpreted as a population effect.

sec.title: 5.4. Measurement instrument
sec.p: All indicators are measured on five-point Likert scales ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). DTC and BC each comprise four lower-order dimensions measured by four items each, and SBP comprises three pillars measured by four items each. The instrument therefore contains 44 items and eleven lower-order constructs (Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5).

sec.p: The items were developed for this framework by translating construct definitions from the digital twin, competitiveness and sustainability literatures into statements specific to manufacturing and digital twin use. They are conceptually adapted rather than reproduced from previously validated scales. The “conceptual basis” column in Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5 identifies the sources whose definitions informed each dimension. Because the items have not yet undergone expert content validation, cognitive pre-testing or pilot testing, the instrument should be regarded as a proposed instrument. The psychometric statistics reported in Section 6 demonstrate the evaluation procedure; they do not establish the validity of the instrument. Before field administration, the instrument will be reviewed by an expert panel for content validity, pre-tested with manufacturing managers and piloted.

Two features of the item wording require attention in field application. First, item CEC1 attributes cost reductions to “digital capabilities”, which may partly overlap with DTC content. Second, item CEC2 refers to resource and energy efficiency relative to competitors, which is conceptually close to the environmental items ENV1 and ENV3. Both items were nevertheless retained in the illustrative analysis, for three reasons. First, they express the conceptual definition of cost efficiency adopted here (Dalenogare et al., 2018; Porter, 1985). In digitally enabled manufacturing, cost advantages are frequently realised through digital capabilities and through lower resource and energy use per unit of output, so removing the two items would narrow the content domain of the cost-efficiency dimension. Second, the purpose of the illustration is to demonstrate how the instrument as proposed can be estimated and evaluated; removing items post hoc on the basis of illustrative data would not be informative. Third, the discriminant validity diagnostics did not flag the two items in the illustrative data. CEC1 and CEC2 loaded more highly on cost efficiency (0.85 and 0.86) than on any DTC dimension (≤0.34) or on environmental performance (0.27 and 0.32). In addition, the heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) ratios of cost efficiency with the DTC dimensions (≤0.446) and with environmental performance (0.367) were well below 0.85.

These diagnostics cannot, however, rule out that shared wording contributes to the structural estimates. Overlap between CEC1 and DTC would tend to inflate the DTC → BC coefficient. Overlap between CEC2 and the environmental items would tend to inflate the BC → ENV coefficient and, through the aggregate composite, part of the BC → SBP coefficient. Because the two items are only two of the sixteen indicators of the higher-order BC construct, any such inflation is diluted, but it is not removed. The DTC → BC and BC → ENV estimates should therefore be read as potentially upper-bound illustrations. In the field version, CEC1 will be reworded to refer to cost reductions without naming their source, and CEC2 will be reworded to refer to unit cost rather than to resource and energy efficiency. The model will also be estimated with and without these items as a robustness check.

sec.title: 5.5. Measurement model specification
sec.p: All constructs of the first order are explicitly constructed. Each item in each dimension is supposed to be a different expression of the same dimension, so that a change in the dimension should be manifested in all of the items, and the items should be highly correlated (Jarvis et al., 2003).

DTC and BC are defined as reflective-reflective higher order constructs (Sarstedt et al., 2019). These four dimensions for DTC are hypothesized as being the levels of capability. Modelling competence and integration know-how are shared within the firm, and a firm with higher modelling competence and know-how is expected to be better at the other three functions, so that the dimensions are expected to co-vary. The same rationale goes for BC’s size, which is expected to be proportional to the overall competitiveness of the firm. If the dimensions were supposed to vary independently of each other and together to define the construct, a reflective–formative specification would be more appropriate. The correlations within the DTC dimensions (0.532–0.627) and within the BC dimensions (0.513–0.565) are consistent with the reflective–reflective specification as shown in the illustrative data. This specification should be tested for validity in field data and a reflective–formative specification should be estimated as a robustness check.

This is a different situation for SBP. The four pillars are conceptually different domains of outcomes, and not all are expected to covary, suggesting that in theory a reflective–formative specification of the aggregate SBP construct is more appropriate. In the illustrative estimation, SBP was estimated as a reflective higher order construct in the second stage, to get the aggregate outcome for H2–H4. In the illustrative data, however, the social pillar was almost uncorrelated with the environmental (r = 0.084) and governance pillars (r = 0.041). Hence, the SBP composite is not very sensitive to the social pillar and has to be analyzed primarily as an environmental–governance composite. Thus, there is a need to avoid using the disaggregated (pillar-level) specification for testing H5–H7 as it will be more informative about sustainability outcomes, and a reflective–formative specification of SBP is recommended for field use.

Despite the above, the aggregate model for H2–H4 is still used as it has three analytical functions. First, it is a general question on the DTC to SBP route. To check if the pathway is direct, indirect or both, only one outcome is required, and the magnitude and the direction of the total, direct and indirect effect of DTC can be decomposed and compared in the same mediation test (H3 and H4). Second, many studies on digitalisation and sustainability use composite sustainability or ESG measures (e.g., Jin & Wu, 2024) and the aggregate model reveals what would be the result of applying such a composite to the proposed framework. Third, the results at the pillar level are interpreted in the context of the aggregate model. It can be compared to the disaggregated specification to illustrate how a composite outcome can show a positive competitiveness–sustainability relationship, but not apply that relationship to a pillar to which it does not extend. The aggregate model is therefore a parsimonious representation of the overall pathway and is not the first point of reference when interpreting sustainability outcomes, but rather is a standard. The pillar-level analysis (H5–H7) is the more informative one for sustainability, and the discussion and implications in Sections 7 and 8 are mainly based on this analysis.

sec.title: 5.6. Common method variance
sec.p: To reduce the potential for common method variance, procedural remedies are built into the instrument design for the field study: first, the respondents are anonymized; second, predictor and criterion items are separated; and third, the items are balanced in terms of wording (Podsakoff et al., 2003). Since the illustrative data set does not include respondent-generated data, common method issue in the substantive sense is not a concern in the present estimation. An independent full-collinearity assessment was however performed (Kock, 2015) to provide the diagnostic. Unlike the collinearity assessment of the structural model presented in Section 6.3.1, in this test each construct in the model is regressed on all other constructs in the model. The variance inflation factors (VIFs) for all variables were less than 3.3 in the full-collinearity test and the maximum VIF at an indicator-level was 2.81. These diagnostics should be supplemented by a marker-variable approach in the field application, and where possible, by several informants and/or archival sustainability indicators.

sec.title: 5.7. Analytical procedure
sec.p: The model was estimated with PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4 (Ringle et al., 2022) using the path-weighting scheme. PLS-SEM is appropriate for three reasons: the model combines higher-order constructs and mediation, the approach is prediction-oriented, and it does not require multivariate normality (Hair et al., 2019; Hair et al., 2022). The higher-order constructs were estimated using the disjoint two-stage approach, in which latent variable scores of the lower-order dimensions obtained in the first stage serve as indicators of the higher-order constructs in the second stage (Becker et al., 2023; Sarstedt et al., 2019).

The measurement model was evaluated through indicator loadings (≥0.708), internal consistency reliability (Cronbach’s α, ρA, and composite reliability ρc) and convergent validity (average variance extracted, AVE ≥ 0.50). Discriminant validity was assessed with the Fornell–Larcker criterion, the HTMT ratio with a conservative threshold of 0.85, and cross-loadings (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Franke & Sarstedt, 2019; Henseler et al., 2015). The structural model was evaluated through collinearity (inner VIF), path coefficients with bootstrapped percentile confidence intervals (CIs) (1,000 subsamples), R² and adjusted R², effect sizes f² (Cohen, 1988) and Stone–Geisser’s Q² obtained by blindfolding. The standardised root mean square residual (SRMR) and the normed fit index (NFI) are reported as approximate indicators of model fit. Because their use in PLS-SEM remains debated, they are not treated as decisive evidence (Hair et al., 2019). For field estimation, 10,000 bootstrap subsamples and out-of-sample predictive assessment using PLSpredict are recommended (Hair et al., 2022; Shmueli et al., 2019).

Mediation was assessed by bootstrapping the indirect effect (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). Mediation is inferred when the CI of the indirect effect excludes zero, and the mediation pattern is classified from the significance of the direct effect (Alzubi, 2025; Nitzl et al., 2016). The variance accounted for (VAF) is reported only as a descriptive indicator of the share of the total effect transmitted indirectly; it is not used to classify mediation.

H5–H7 were tested in the disaggregated specification, in which the aggregate SBP construct is replaced by its three pillars as separate endogenous constructs. Each pillar is predicted by BC, and the direct path from DTC to each pillar is retained so that the pillar-level competitiveness coefficients are estimated net of any direct DTC effect. These direct DTC–pillar paths are not hypothesised.

sec.title: 6. Results of the illustrative estimation
sec.p: All results in this section derive from the 418-case illustrative dataset. They demonstrate the evaluation of the proposed framework and should not be interpreted as estimates for any population of manufacturing firms.

sec.title: 6.1. Descriptive statistics and item-level assessment
sec.p: Table 6 reports the means, standard deviations, skewness, kurtosis and outer loadings of all items. Item means ranged from 3.35 to 3.71, and standard deviations ranged from 0.83 to 0.92. Skewness (−0.38 to 0.01) and kurtosis (−0.65 to 0.08) were well within the conventional limits of ±2 and ±7, respectively. All outer loadings exceeded the 0.708 threshold (range: 0.776–0.903), indicating satisfactory indicator reliability in the illustrative data.

caption.title: Item-level descriptive statistics and outer loadings (illustrative dataset, N = 418)

sec.title: 6.2.1 Internal consistency reliability and convergent validity
sec.p: Table 7 summarises reliability and convergent validity for the eleven lower-order constructs. Cronbach’s α (0.854–0.903), ρA (0.855–0.923) and composite reliability ρc (0.901–0.932) exceeded 0.70, and all AVE values exceeded 0.50 (0.695–0.773) (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Hair et al., 2019).

caption.title: Construct reliability and convergent validity (illustrative dataset)

sec.title: 6.2.2 Discriminant validity
sec.p: Discriminant validity was supported by all three criteria (Franke & Sarstedt, 2019; Henseler et al., 2015). The square root of each construct’s AVE exceeded its correlations with all other constructs (Table 8). All HTMT ratios were below the conservative threshold of 0.85, with a maximum of 0.727 (Table 9). Each indicator also loaded more highly on its own construct than on any other construct (Table 10). The correlations of the social pillar with all other constructs were close to zero (−0.070 to 0.084), a feature of the illustrative data that is relevant to the interpretation of H6.

sec.title: 6.3.1 Collinearity
sec.p: Table 11 reports the inner VIF values of the structural model, which assess collinearity among the predictors of each endogenous construct. These values are distinct from the full-collinearity VIFs used as a common method variance diagnostic in Section 5.6, which were obtained from a separate assessment in which each construct is regressed on all other constructs. All inner VIF values were well below 3.3, indicating that collinearity among the predictors was not a concern.

sec.title: 6.3.2 Explanatory power and predictive relevance
sec.p: Table 12 reports R², adjusted R² and Q². The model explained 29.3% of the variance in BC and 22.9% of the variance in SBP. In the disaggregated specification, it explained 21.8% of the variance in environmental performance and 21.3% of the variance in governance performance. These values are weak by conventional benchmarks (Hair et al., 2019), which is plausible for a parsimonious model in which each outcome has at most two predictors. All Q² values were positive except that for social performance. For the social pillar, R² was effectively zero (0.000) and Q² was slightly negative (−0.009), indicating that the model had neither explanatory power nor predictive relevance for social performance in the illustrative data. This result is examined further in the test of H6 and in Section 7.5.

caption.title: Coefficient of determination (R²), adjusted R² and predictive relevance (Q²) (illustrative dataset)

sec.title: 6.3.3 Effect sizes
sec.p: As shown in Table 13, DTC had a large effect on BC (f² = 0.414). BC had medium effects on SBP (f² = 0.181) and on environmental performance (f² = 0.184) and a small effect on governance performance (f² = 0.139). The effects of DTC on SBP (f² = 0.003) and of BC on social performance (f² = 0.000) were negligible (Cohen, 1988).

sec.title: 6.3.4 Model fit
sec.p: The SRMR (0.038) was below the commonly used threshold of 0.08, and the NFI was 0.985 (Table 14). Fit indices in PLS-SEM are approximate, and the data are illustrative. These values therefore indicate only that the specified model reproduces the illustrative correlation matrix; they are not evidence of the validity of the model for manufacturing firms (Hair et al., 2019).

sec.title: 6.3.5 Direct effects
sec.p: Table 15 reports the bootstrapped direct effects. DTC was positively and significantly associated with BC (β = 0.541, t = 16.49, p &lt; 0.001), and BC was positively and significantly associated with SBP (β = 0.444, t = 10.18, p &lt; 0.001). The illustrative estimation was therefore consistent with H1 and H2. The direct effect of DTC on SBP was not significant (β = 0.059, t = 1.18, p = 0.238; 95% CI [−0.04, 0.16]), so H3 was not supported within the illustrative estimation.

At the pillar level, BC was positively and significantly associated with environmental performance (β = 0.452, t = 8.98, p &lt; 0.001) and governance performance (β = 0.394, t = 8.20, p &lt; 0.001), so the illustrative estimation was consistent with H5 and H7. By contrast, the association between BC and social performance was close to zero and not significant (β = 0.023, t = 0.37, p = 0.713; 95% CI [−0.10, 0.15]), so H6 was not supported within the illustrative estimation.

sec.title: 6.3.6 Mediation analysis
sec.p: Table 16 shows specific indirect effect of DTC on SBP via BC. The indirect effect was positive and significant (β = 0.240, t = 8.53, p < 0.001), and its 95% bootstrap CI [0.19, 0.30] excluded zero. The illustrative estimation was thus in line with H4. There was no direct effect of DTC on SBP, so that an indirect effect only was obtained, also known as full mediation (Nitzl et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2010), sometimes referred to as partial mediation. The total effect (0.300) was split into indirect (0.300 × 80.2%) and mediated (0.300 × 20.0%). This VAF value is not used in the classification of the mediation, but is reported descriptively. The pattern shown is illustrative, as the data are cross-sectional, and not a causal finding of transmission of the effect of DTC in manufacturing firms through BC.

caption.title: Mediation analysis: Specific indirect effect (illustrative dataset)

sec.title: 6.3.7 Summary of hypothesis tests
sec.p: The estimated structural model is presented in Figure 2, and the hypotheses decisions are summarised in Table 17. The illustrative estimation supported the five hypotheses (H1, H2, H4, H5 and H7), but not the other two (H3 and H6). The decisions made are based only on the illustrative estimation and are not an empirical confirmation.
