sec.title: 7. Discussion
sec.p: In this study, it was aimed to determine how DTC can contribute to SBP and if that path goes all the way to all of the ESG pillars. This section will explain what the pattern of the estimates would have theoretically meant if it had been seen in field data, and how the pattern compares with previous research in this field since it is based on illustrative data. It does not regard the estimates as actual conclusions about manufacturing firms.

sec.title: 7.1. Digital twin capability and business competitiveness
sec.p: The illustrative estimation revealed a very high positive correlation between DTC and BC (Table 15). Theoretically, the three functions of monitoring, sensing and simulation, decision-support and seizing, and synchronisation and reconfiguring of a digital twin generate competitive value (Teece, 2007; Warner & Wäger, 2019). The pattern in terms of directionality is consistent with the evidence that has been presented in the literature in which the innovation of digital twins has been found to be associated with the operational performance of the firm (Li et al., 2026) and the use of the digital twins with the performance of the supply-chain (Singh et al., 2023). It is also aligned with findings that operational performance is related to digital transformation in Jordanian manufacturers (Almajali et al., 2025). This framework builds on the work by defining the capability at the level of adoption, which has been extended to the level of four functional dimensions. Two cautions apply. First, the numeric value of the illustrative coefficient does not provide any information on the actual magnitude of the relationship. Second, one cost-efficiency item is clearly digital related, so field research is needed to ensure the association does not stem from some of the content being duplicated across the items.

sec.title: 7.2. Business competitiveness and sustainable business performance
sec.p: In the illustrative estimation, the association with the aggregate SBP was positive for BC (Table 15). Theoretically, this pattern could be said to reinforce the legitimacy and operational discipline and slack of the competitive firms to institutionalize sustainability practices (Hart, 1995). Additionally, this is in line with the suggestion by Ghobakhloo (2020) that the economic roles of Industry 4.0 come before the environmental and social roles of the industry. It is not the same as ordering examined by Fan et al. (2025) where ESG is positioned between digital technology application and competitiveness. The two orderings do not contradict each other, and reciprocal relationships are possible over time, but the only data available at the time is a cross-sectional view. Furthermore, from the illustrative data (Section 5.5) there was not a lot of variation between social and the other pillars, so the overall association between BC and SBP is largely a reflection of the environmental and governance pillars. The overall pathway is best interpreted using the overall pathway result, which is the aggregate of all pillars, whereas the sustainability interpretation is more informative and is provided in Section 7.4–7.6 at the pillar level.

sec.title: 7.3. Direct versus indirect pathways from digital twin capability to sustainable business performance
sec.p: The pathway from DTC to SBP can be direct or indirect.

The illustrative estimation showed that the direct DTC→SBP path was small and insignificant while the indirect path through BC was significant (Table 15 and Table 16). This appears to be an indirect-only mediation pattern (Zhao et al., 2010). In theory, it’s aligned with the digital transformation assertion that it is the act of adapting organisational routines and not the digital adoption itself that leads to performance outcomes (Verhoef et al., 2021; Vial, 2019). It also aligns with the worry that “automatic” sustainability potential of digitalisation is not realised (Lange et al., 2020). The pattern also echoes previous studies where the sustainability outcomes of digitalisation are mediated by other capabilities, including dynamic capabilities (Jin & Wu, 2024), green innovation (Li et al., 2025) and supply-chain resilience and performance (Singh et al., 2023). The purpose of the framework is to define BC as a sustainability-relevant conversion mechanism and illustrate the role of the conversion mechanism in the context of a direct technical pathway.

This pattern must be viewed with care, though. Non-significant direct effects in an illustrative data set does not imply that there is no direct sustainability effect from digital twins. At the asset and process level, there are examples of direct energy and resource savings (Ma et al., 2022; Zeynivand et al., 2025) that might not be reflected in perceptual, firm-level outcome metrics. Whether the direct path is negligible, and whether any other mediators act in parallel to BC is a question that can only be answered through field research.

sec.title: 7.4. Environmental performance
sec.p: For the disaggregated specification, BC was positively related to environmental performance. Theoretically, the pattern makes sense because competitiveness and environmental performance both focus on efficiency and share a common foundation of resource productivity: Smaller amounts of energy and materials used to produce each unit of goods reduce costs and environmental impacts. The overall picture is consistent with the case evidence of energy and environmental cost reduction based on digital-twin enabled production management (Ma et al., 2022), and reviews locating resource efficiency as a key element of the contribution of the digital-twin to sustainability (He & Bai, 2021; Kamble et al., 2022). The conceptual overlap between the cost-efficiency item of resource and energy efficiency (CEC2) and the environmental items (Section 5.4) may be part of this association. Finally, field research can be used to evaluate the validity of the BC prediction of environmental outcomes where the two constructs are measured with well-differentiated content, ideally including archival measures like energy intensity or waste per unit of product.

sec.title: 7.5. Social performance
sec.p: The social pathway differed from the others. As reported in Section 6.3 (Table 12, Table 13, and Table 15), BC did not significantly explain social performance in the illustrative estimation, and the model had neither explanatory power nor predictive relevance for this pillar. This is a non-significant pathway, not evidence of a negative social consequence, and it does not establish that social outcomes are systematically decoupled from competitiveness in manufacturing firms.

The contrast with the environmental and governance pathways is nevertheless theoretically informative. Environmental and governance outcomes share a routine base with competitiveness, because they are produced, at least in part, by the same efficiency, quality and control routines that a digital twin reorganises. Lower energy and material use per unit of output reduces both costs and environmental burdens. Similarly, the traceability and documentation needed to serve demanding customers reliably also underpin transparent reporting and risk management. Social outcomes lack this shared base, because they are produced mainly by human-resource, safety and participation routines that lie outside the operational domain in which digital twins act. For the proposed framework, this implies that BC should be understood as a selective rather than a general conversion mechanism: its reach is bounded by the overlap between the routines it strengthens and the routines that generate each sustainability outcome. Extending the framework to social outcomes is therefore likely to require a complementary mechanism, such as human-centric work design and workforce capability building (Xu et al., 2021), rather than stronger competitiveness alone.

If a similar pattern were observed in field data, several explanations would merit examination. First, social performance may depend more strongly on factors not included in the model than on competitiveness itself. Such factors include human-resource practices, workforce development, employee participation, occupational safety management systems and organisational culture (Xu et al., 2021). Human-resource strategies have been shown to shape digital transformation, with sustainability practices moderating that effect (Allahham et al., 2025), and workplace factors drive the innovative work behaviour of employees, an effect conditioned by an innovative organisational culture (Alshami et al., 2026). Second, labour regulation and institutional conditions may shape social outcomes largely independently of a firm’s competitive position, which would make the social pillar more responsive to regulatory and institutional variation than to market performance. Third, efficiency-driven competitiveness may simultaneously create resources for social investment and pressures towards work intensification, producing offsetting effects that sum to approximately zero (Kovacs, 2018; Narkhede et al., 2024). Fourth, the social scale combines workplace safety, employee development, community contribution and labour practices, which may respond differently to competitiveness. Finally, because of the illustrative-data design, the pattern cannot be attributed to any real-world mechanism. Distinguishing among these explanations requires field data, a richer set of organisational and institutional variables and, possibly, separate modelling of the components of social performance.

sec.title: 7.6. Governance performance
sec.p: The illustrative estimation showed positive association with BC and governance performance. In theory, it supports the hypothesis that competitive firms that cater to high-quality customers have an institutionalized process that makes transparency, accountability, and risk-management easier; and that data-rich operations facilitate the institutionalization of these processes. Research that developed digital transformation capability offers a path for manufacturers to enhance their ESG performance is consistent (Jin & Wu, 2024). The framework also introduces the idea that governance goals can be achieved by the competitiveness pathway as well as through technology. Documentary evidence, such as sustainability reporting, a certified management system, or lack thereof, could also be used to assess governance performance in field research, which would help address the need to rely on self-reported perceptions.

The illustrative estimation demonstrates that the framework is able to pinpoint an indirect pathway from a direct pathway and that it is capable of identifying differences in the way in which the ESG pillars react to competitiveness. The difference between the environmental and governance pathways and the social pathway would have been masked by a composite SBP measure alone. It is the main methodological innovation of this framework with respect to the assessment of the sustainability impacts of digitalisation.

sec.title: 8.1. Theoretical implications
sec.p: The framework has three theoretical implications. The framework has three theoretical implications. Firstly, it moves the digital twin from the technological level to the level of the firm, introducing four dimensions that are functionally organised, and it dissociates the digital twin from its enabling conditions. The difference between these gives insight into how different digital twin solutions could lead to varying sustainability results in firms and makes a distinction from the level of general Industry 4.0 capability.

Second, the framework combines three theoretical lenses into a single causal chain with each lens having a distinct role. The resource-based view helps to understand the strategic value of DTC, the dynamic capability theory explains the transformation of strategic value to a competitive advantage and finally, digital transformation theory is used to understand the transformation of competitive and organisational change to sustainability outcomes. This integration is the mechanism by means of which digital capability is linked with SBP and points to the direct technological mechanism as a competing explanation that can be tested empirically.

Third, clarifying the link between SBP, ESG and the triple bottom line and modelling the ESG pillars separately also makes explicit the potential that digitalisation can drive competitiveness in some dimensions of sustainability, but not others. It thus brings together research on digital capability and the potential negatively perceived impacts of Industry 4.0 on sustainability, as seen by Narkhede et al. (2024). It also provides a design to study the circumstances in which digitalisation can and cannot help to create sustainable manufacturing.

These implications represent three advances that differ from the literature in digital twins sustainability reviewed in Section 2.1. The framework progresses from technology to capability. Both engineering and case and review studies provide insight into the functions of a digital twin at the asset and process level (He & Bai, 2021; Kamble et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022; Zeynivand et al., 2025); only a few firm-level studies quantify digital twin adoption or innovations (Li et al., 2026; Singh et al., 2023). The current mechanisms, on the other hand, identify a four dimensional, firm level DTC, which is distinct from its conditions. Second, the framework shifts from an assumption of direct impacts to a clear conversion mechanism. The previous research either assumes that sustainability benefits will be achieved as a direct result of the digital twin functionality or connects digitalisation with sustainability via supply chain resilience and performance (Singh et al., 2023) or general dynamic capabilities (Jin & Wu, 2024). The present framework, however, states that the conversion mechanism is BC and compares it to the direct technological pathway in one model. Third, the framework shifts from aggregate to pillar level outcomes. Existing research tends to focus on environmental outcomes or composite sustainability and ESG indices, whereas the current framework looks at the three aspects of sustainability (environmental, social, and governance) separately, and thus reveals unequal outcomes that are not discovered by composites. There is no need to develop any additional theory for these advances—they can simply be deduced from how the existing lenses are brought together and put into practice.

sec.title: 8.2. Human resource management at the workplace
sec.p: Since no field observations were analysed, the implications below are based on the logic of the proposed framework, not on the illustrative coefficients, and all will need to be empirically tested and validated before they could provide guidance for managerial practice. The framework also suggests that the potential sustainability impact of a digital twin might not be as dependent on technology as on the capability to be developed on top of it, encompassing data infrastructure, integration knowledge and decision routines in all four dimensions. If this is accepted, then digital twin projects may be considered to be capability-enhancing programmes instead of technology buying.

Secondly, if field research verifies that BC plays a role in a conversion process, then metrics like unit cost, delivery reliability, defect rates, speed of technological adoption could be used as steps along the path of assessing whether digital twin investments will create environmental and governance benefits. Firms could evaluate both pathways by measuring these indicators in addition to measuring their own resource efficiency. This is a proposition that is not a monitoring rule set by the current estimates, it is based on the causal logic of the framework.

Third, the theoretical underpinning of the framework (Section 4.5) points to the fact that competitiveness can be insufficient to enhance social performance and the illustrative pathway of social performance does not confirm this. If the results of the field research were to verify this, companies aiming to make a step forward in social sustainability would have to implement explicit actions, including reskilling, job redesign, occupational safety programmes and participative change management, alongside the adoption of digital twins, and not rely on the social benefits automatically following the competitive benefits. Pillar-level field evidence should not be used to claim that digital twins provide consistent ESG benefits until it is available, otherwise technology providers and consultants should not make such claims.

sec.title: 8.3. Sustainability and policy implications
sec.p: The proposed framework has three implications for sustainable-manufacturing policy. They are provided as guidance for policy dialogue which needs empirical testing and are not the policy recommendations determined by the illustrative coefficients. The framework suggests that public support for industrial digitalisation (e.g., shared test-beds, co-funding and readiness programmes) could be more effective in advancing sustainability when combined with capability development and measurable environmental outcomes, for example energy or material intensity, and not only with technology purchase. Second, if field research shows that digitalisation is not necessarily a social sustainable path on its own, policy makers may want to combine the incentives of digitalisation with the workforce-development and occupational-safety conditions, ensuring that the social pillar does not suffer while increasing productivity. Third, in the event of validation of the proposed governance pathway, policy could support environmental reporting and traceability based on data. Such interventions would have to take into account the different levels of readiness for digital transformation that firms have, as in emerging-economy countries like Jordan.

sec.title: 9. Limitations and future research
sec.p: The study comes with a number of limitations that circumscribe its contribution.

First, and above all, the empirical part does not rely on observations taken in the field, but on an illustrative dataset (N = 418). Estimates illustrate how the framework could be implemented and assessed but offer no evidence of the existence, sign or strength of the proposed links between manufacturing firms. However, the numerical estimates cannot be extrapolated to the application context of the intended users of this study, namely the Jordanian manufacturers, which have not been studied yet. Patterns noted in the data were generated to illustrate the data rather than as discoveries: the indirect-only mediation and the non-significant social pathway.

Secondly, the design is cross sectional. Even when using field data, a cross-sectional design cannot rule out reverse causation and reciprocal causation between competitiveness and sustainability performance (Fan et al., 2025). Bootstrapped mediation test is to determine if an indirect effect is statistically significant, not causal.

Thirdly, the model is deliberately parsimonious and excludes potentially important variables. These include the enabling conditions of DTC (interoperability, data integration quality, IT infrastructure, organisational readiness and digital skills), contextual moderators (firm size, sub-sector, regulatory pressure and institutional environment) and determinants of social performance (human-resource practices, employee participation, occupational safety systems and labour regulation). The estimated paths might be biased if there are omitted variables in field applications.

Fourth, the measuring instrument has not been validated yet. These items are conceptualized and need to be content validated and pre-tested by experts. There are constructs that have overlapping content with other constructs: One item of cost-efficiency addresses digital skills, and another addresses resource and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the outcome measures are perceptual and in the planned field design would be provided by single key informants. Reworking the treatment of SBP as a reflective higher order construct is also warranted, as the ESG pillars do not necessarily co-vary (Section 5.5).

Fifth, some analytical decisions are related to the demonstrative nature of the study. Field estimation should be based on 10,000 bootstrap subsamples, out-of-sample prediction should be evaluated using PLSpredict and fit indices should be treated with caution (Hair et al., 2022; Shmueli et al., 2019).

As indicated by these restraints, there are clear research directions to be pursued. The focus is on estimating the framework based on data gathered from manufacturing companies in Jordan through a stratified sampling protocol as described in Section 5.2 and based on the content-validated instrument and, if possible, more than one informant and archival indicators of the ESG performance. The model should also be applied to other manufacturing sub-sectors and to other emerging economy settings for comparison to determine if context is a factor. Longitudinal designs would enable the sequence of competitiveness and sustainability performance to be explored. Social-sustainability-related factors such as human-resource management, employee participation, occupational-safety systems and labour regulations should be modeled as antecedents or moderators for future studies. In addition to BC, competing and complementary metrics like ESG performance, green innovation and supply chain resilience can be measured (Fan et al., 2025; Jin & Wu, 2024; Singh et al., 2023). Last, but not least, the relative impact of the four dimensions of DTC and the importance of enabling conditions (such as interoperability, digital skills etc.) needs to be explored.

sec.title: 10. Conclusions
sec.p: This study created an SBP-involving framework that elucidates the contribution of DTC in the manufacturing context from a sustainability perspective. It is based on the premise that digitalisation is never sustainable by itself. Digital twins’ technical potential to cut resource consumption, predict failure, and enhance control must first be translated into organizational results before it can impact ESG performance. The framework looks at DTC as a capability at the firm level, conceptualising it as four-dimensional: the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory are combined in a single causal logic. In this logic, BC is proposed as the mechanism to get to sustainability outcomes while SBP is operationalised by the ESG pillars that are separate from the economic content of competitiveness.

The framework was implemented and tested in the illustrative analysis of 418 cases, which showed that the framework could be operationalized and evaluated using existing procedures. The difference was found to be indirect-only mediation in the illustrative data as the effect of DTC was transmitted via BC and not directly. The relationship between BC and environmental and governance performance were found at the pillar level but were not found with social performance. They show what it aims to identify: sustainability returns to digital capability based on competitive conversion, and that it is unevenly distributed across the ESG pillars. They fail to exhibit the same patterns among manufacturing firms.

The framework is thus able to provide a theoretically-based and empirically verifiable explanation of the situations in which digitalisation can, and can’t, contribute to sustainable manufacturing. However, for its intended application context of Jordanian manufacturing companies, field validation is needed to confirm the pathway to sustainability value of competitiveness and to determine whether there are mechanisms available to create sustainability beyond competitiveness.
